More than 70% of researchers have tried and failed to reproduce another scientist's experiments, and more than half have failed to reproduce their own experiments.

What this means is that nearly 7 in 10 so-called scientists are not utilizing the scientific method at all.

Not even remotely correct. There are many, many reasons behind this failure to reproduce and moral corruption or whatever this blogger is trying to insinuate is not a major reason.

The biggest reason is probably statistics. The universe is full of randomness. Take a fair coin, one with a 50/50 chance of landing heads or tails, and toss it 10 times. It might come up tails each time. You know that it would be quite rare for that to happen with a fair coin (1 in 1,024 chance), so based on this "experiment," you might conclude that this coin does not seem to be fair, and is instead weighted. This would be pretty interesting and you'd want to tell other people that this coin is weighted. When someone goes to repeat this experiment, they'll probably find that the coin landed tails-up 4-6 times out of 10, conclude that the coin actually is fair, and say that they failed to replicate your results. But you didn't lie. You didn't cheat. You didn't mess up how you flipped it. You just got (un)lucky and had something rare happen.

This happens a lot in science. We have a cutoff point where we say, "This result is unlikely to happen due to pure chance, and so there is probably a reason behind it." The chance of something happening randomly can be quantified with a p-value (probability value). When p is less than 0.05, that means there is less than a 5% chance that this result is the product of randomness, and is not due to a real difference. Going back to the coin example, the chance of flipping 10 tails in a row is 1 in 1,024, so p = 0.000977. We know the coin was actually fair, but you were completely justified in saying that you did not believe it was.

Now the same stuff happens in science. Say you're comparing one cancer drug to another, and these drugs are actually equally effective, but we don't know this yet. You give Drug A to 20 samples of tumors and you give Drug B to 20 different samples of the same type of tumor. If Drug A kills 17 of those samples and Drug B only kills 11, there is only a 3.92% chance of that happening if the drugs were equally effective. p = 0.0392, which is less than our cutoff point of 0.05. So you say there is a significant difference between these drugs and publish your paper. Cancer researchers are excited about this result and try to replicate the results. They fail, because you were (un)lucky and had a rare occurrence. But if 100 researchers repeated the experiment, 3 or 4 of them would get the same results you did, because there's an element of chance here, just like when flipping a coin.

Examples like this don't show that modern science, or "science" as this blogger would probably say, is broken. Instead it stresses the importance of repeating experiments to try to replicate results. This doesn't happen as often as it should, for many reasons, but it does still happen. Especially when a finding is particularly groundbreaking or weird, many independent scientists will see if they can get the same result or not. Be critical, take everything with a grain of salt, and by all means go read the original article instead of relying on the sensationalized media retelling, but you can still trust science.

It takes monumentally more effort to refute bullshit than to create it, and I want to thank you for taking the time to write this post in a way that most people can understand. Sure, there is also some bias in science and some instances of people failing to isolate variables, but most scientists truly are trying their damndest to adhere to these scientific rulesets.

At the end of the day everyone learns from the mistakes and science progresses.

Science doesn't need all papers to be good. It doesn't even need most papers to be good. As long as the work is honest (it might get embellished a bit, but actual fraud is extremely rare) then everyone will learn.

An expert will be familiar with that context and be able to adequately interpret and judge a paper. But for a layman this is dangerous.
